evening.title: Security forces conduct anti-Fidayeen attack drill at railway station in Kulgam
evening.text:
Police, in coordination with the Army, railway police and CRPF, conducted an anti-Fidayeen attack drill on Wednesday at a railway station in Jammu and Kashmir’s Kulgam district, officials said.
“Kulgam Police, in coordination with the Army, GRP, RPF and CRPF, conducted an anti-fidayeen mock drill at Harnag Railway Station to assess operational preparedness and inter-agency coordination,” a police spokesperson said.
During the exercise, road cut-offs were established at designated locations, and participating agencies carried out coordinated response measures to neutralise the simulated threat and ensure the safe evacuation of passengers and civilians, he said.
The exercise aimed to enhance operational readiness, improve response time and strengthen coordination among security agencies to ensure an effective response to any eventuality, he added.
Handwara SSP Sajad Khaliq Bhat reviewed the security and operational preparedness in the North Kashmir police district.
Bhat, who assumed charge on Monday, undertook a detailed review of critical security and policing aspects, including investigation of cases under the NDPS and the UAPA Acts, identification of security hotspots, vulnerability mapping, deployment arrangements, law-and-order preparedness and preventive security measures.
He directed officers to strengthen the security grid, intensify patrolling and naka checking, maintain heightened vigilance at sensitive locations and ensure timely preventive action against elements likely to disturb peace and public order.
Bhat also stressed the importance of effective surveillance outside prisons, in accordance with established legal procedures, to identify and prevent potential security threats.
Emphasising the importance of social media surveillance, the SSP directed officers to closely monitor online platforms for provocative, misleading and unlawful content that could affect public peace and security, and to initiate appropriate action in accordance with law.

evening.title: KDE hits 30, decides it's time to move out of the X11 era
evening.text: KDE is marking its 30th birthday by showing X11 sessions the door. The newly released KDE Plasma 6.8 is Wayland-only, though X11 applications can still run through XWayland. The change arrives right on schedule after last month's beta. KWin handles both window management and display-server duties. That means X11-based screen-recording tools, for example, won't work any more. You can't "shade" windows – roll them up into the title bar and back – and that's not planned to come back. Restoring saved sessions can also behave differently. Applications cannot freely position their own windows under Wayland, leaving placement to the compositor. Saying that, there are lots of tweaks and refinements in this release. The Spectacle screenshot tool can now include system audio and microphone input in its screen recordings. Plasma 6.8 integrates with non-KDE tools better. For instance, KDE's browser integration now supports the Flatpak version of Microsoft's Edge browser. GTK2 applications also get better dark-theme matching. Internationalization is getting better – for example, the Clock understands the Bikram Sambat calendar, and Amharic is now supported in KDE's on-screen keyboard. The System Monitor app has better tracking of VRAM usage as well as main memory, and can pin tasks to certain CPU cores. There's better multi-monitor handling: screens are color-coded as well as by make and model, which is helpful if you have multiple identical monitors. There are more authentication options in KDE's VPN support too. The Union theming system is in beta, though not enabled by default. KWin can also apply matching effects to windows with client-side decorations, such as Valve's Steam client. Plasma's High Dynamic Range (HDR) support is better: it follows ICC color profiles, and understands Hybrid Log Gamma. On Nvidia GPUs, Plasma 6.8 enables triple-buffered output, resulting in smoother animations and transitions. Speaking of animations, more system effects – such as desktop "peek" and window "aperture" (when windows slide to the edge of the screen out of the way) – now respect the global animation settings. The Wayland-only session requires alternatives to remote-access tools that depend on an X11 desktop session, but the built-in Remote Desktop server, based on KRdp, has been improved. It's faster, it can adapt to slower connections on the fly, the clipboard is now bi-directional between host and remote system, and an exclusive mode can lock the host's screen while providing a virtual display sized to the client's window. KRdp uses Microsoft's Remote Desktop Protocol, but there's also Krfb if you prefer VNC instead. If you really need individual remote Wayland applications over SSH, then Waypipe is the way to go. The full changelog has all the details of the changes. Kubuntu 27.04 – recently announced as being codenamed "Tenacious T-Rex" – should include Plasma 6.8 when it arrives in April next year. KDE's internal metrics showed more than 95 percent of Plasma 6.6 users running Wayland in June. Including older versions, adoption was about 76 percent. Even so, we suspect that some users won't be happy with this change. With 6.8 out of the door, and on its way into fast-moving distros near you, the SonicDE project, which aims to continue development of the X11-capable KWin from Plasma 6.7, may start to pick up more interest. The KDE Project started with founder Matthias Ettrich's announcement on the de.comp.os.linux newsgroup on October 14, 1996. Before KDE, there were some commercial proprietary Unix desktop environments that were ported to Linux. For instance, Caldera OpenLinux 1.0 shipped with Visix's Looking Glass – you can see a tiny screenshot of it in the OpenLinux 1.1 announcement – but none ever went FOSS. Xfce is slightly older – as founder Olivier Fourdan described in this 2009 article: "I started the project in late 1996, before GNOME or gtk+ even existed." The XForms Common Environment was released first, but in those early days, what was then called XFce wasn't open source. It also started out as a recreation of CDE, which was finally open sourced in 2012. This makes it an early equivalent of NsCDE, which we compared with the real thing in 2022. In its early days, the Qt C++ toolkit that KDE chose caused problems, which led to the establishment of the KDE Free Qt Foundation in case something bad happened to its creators. Qt's licensing situation improved in 2000, when Qt 2.2 became available under both the GPL and QPL, resolving the GPL-compatibility concerns surrounding KDE's foundations. Even holdout Red Hat started bundling KDE. Thirty years on, KDE remains one of the great survivors of the free desktop. Long may it continue. ®

evening.title: When faster supercomputers aren’t enough
evening.text: When a million veterans shared their genetic data by enrolling in the Department of Veterans Affairs' “Million Veteran Program,” they expected nothing back. This did not surprise Ravi Madduri, a senior scientist with the Data Science and Learning Division at the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Argonne National Laboratory. He is abundantly clear about the terms under which these veterans donated their data: “Even after giving everything to the country, they found it in their hearts to give more without expecting anything in return.” That gift, which constituted the nation’s largest biorepository and most ancestrally varied cohorts of veteran data in the world, created a debt that Madduri, who also holds a joint appointment in the Department of Human Genetics at the University of Chicago, is working to repay. “What I feel when I look at that data is that I have an obligation to deliver to the veterans on their intentions in doing this,” he says. Those intentions, as he reads it, are that others, veteran or not, can benefit from whatever the data can reveal. “We cannot dilly dally,” Madduri says. After arriving at Argonne as a graduate student in 2001, Madduri has spent the last two decades at the intersection of supercomputing and biomedicine, much of the time building the computing that turns the veterans’ data into results impacting areas from post-traumatic stress disorder to heart disease to cancer. He explains that machines have largely held up their end, but the obstacles between precious data and delivered results are not always solved with faster machines. Understanding the challenges is the path toward better science. What the Math Was Unable to Solve Any two human genomes differ at millions of specific positions. A genome-wide association study asks a seemingly simple question across an enormous volume of data. For example, does a given genetic variant travel together with a particular medical condition? On its own, the question is simple. Multiplied across every variant worth testing and every condition recorded in a patient's chart, it becomes an enormous math problem, which is what supercomputers exist to solve. The harder question is whether the code is written to let them. Madduri's team has run this problem on the Summit system at DOE's Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility and on the Aurora system at the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility. On Summit, the team found that the job would not finish on the machine's CPUs. As the cohort grew, the matrix the analysis needed for each group no longer fit in memory, and the job stalled. “We decided to open the box and look at the code,” Madduri said. They found that the issue was not merely a speed problem, but a coding one. The analysis had been written for ordinary processors because that is what the genetics community was running on. Underneath the algorithms, though, the code spent nearly all of its time doing one thing: multiplying very large grids of numbers. This is exactly the operation that graphics processors exist to perform, and what makes them the engine of modern artificial intelligence training. As Madduri notes, the same computational architecture accelerating AI discovery “is also foundational for population genomics.” So, the team, led on this effort by Argonne's Alex Rodriguez, rewrote that part of the code for GPUs, and an analysis that would have taken roughly 481,000 CPU-core hours in the original version became tractable. This shift did more than speed up a slow job. It made a virtually impossible job possible. The workhorse they accelerated is a widely used genetics package called SAIGE, which made the rewritten version SAIGE-GPU, described in a separate paper in Bioinformatics. "We are not good at coming up with names. Sorry," Madduri says sheepishly. Before SAIGE-GPU, nearly every genome-wide association study started by picking a disease then looking for the variants linked to it. Madduri is blunt about the cost of that approach. “One of the challenges I found in biomedical research is that it is very incremental,” he explains. “Every year, they get new datasets, they analyze the data, they find a new set of genetic variants, and this happens across all of the different diseases.” The reason, he adds, is limited access to large-scale computing. His team chose not to be incremental and decided to solve the computational challenge once and for all. “One of the challenges we set for ourselves was to just take all the data that we have available, all the genetic data for all the veterans that have been sequenced as part of the Million Veteran Program,” Madduri says. The team, the Million Veteran Program consortium, published the results in Science, with Madduri's group among the authors, and published the computational work separately in Bioinformatics. The study reported on 2,068 traits across 635,969 veterans, and the results flagged 13,672 regions of the genome linked to one or more conditions. About 1,600 of these regions surfaced only because nearly a third of the participants were not of European ancestry. According to the Science paper, most genetic studies to this point have been drawn overwhelmingly from people of European descent. These 1,600 associations were previously “invisible” in the populations studied. That ancestral range also shaped how the analysis had to be run. The groups could not simply be pooled. That is, if a condition is more common in one ancestral group than another, the analysis has no way to tell a genuine disease marker from a marker of simply belonging to that group. Each group had to be run separately, and the results combined afterward. The 1,600 associations exist in no single group's results. They appear only when the separate analyses are combined. Madduri is careful about what the whole exercise means and what it does not. “This is all preclinical,” he says. “This is the discovery phase.” The analysis produces a statistical map of where to look. Turning any one of those 13,672 regions into a treatment takes years of downstream work by researchers who pick up and follow the data, which is why Madduri says the team never stopped. “Things that took 14 days when we wrote the Science paper now take less than a couple of hours,” he says. While this means getting an answer sooner, the real win is being able to ask the same question of a bigger population “with a larger cohort size and more statistical rigor than the paper that we published a couple of years ago.” When Data Cannot Travel The veterans’ genomes have an unusual advantage over other medical data. One agency gathered the data under one agreement, which is what made bringing them to Summit possible. In medicine, Madduri says, data “cannot be shared with one another as freely as you would probably share cosmology data.” The alternative is to move the model, he says: “Federated learning allows you to train models without moving data around.” This means each institution trains on the copy it already holds, behind its own walls, and only sends back the adjustments the model learned. Those adjustments are combined into a single updated model, which goes out to everyone, and the cycle repeats. Asked how several institutions are persuaded to compute together without pooling anything, he corrects the premise. “It is not the institution,” he says. “The first layer of that puzzle is people wanting to work together, to collaborate.” Then, the part that makes it work: “It is a people federation.” Madduri was a co-developer of APPFL, the Argonne Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning framework, which provides a means to help “move” models rather than data. The machinery underneath is closer to access control than to machine learning. "You do not have to write code for each scheduler," he says. Globus Compute presents one interface across the facilities' schedulers, and APPFL submits its training jobs through it. Even with these technical challenges, the harder problem is permission. “All the computing that happens is authorized computing that is tied to a project allocation,” Madduri says. Federated training means that each collaborator’s job has to run under their own institutional credentials on a machine they are personally entitled to use. A site with data nobody else has makes that shared model better for everyone. "If one site has data that are unique to it and other sites do not have that, then the model becomes more robust," Madduri adds. Many Different Worlds Madduri has been a regular attendee at the SC Conference since SC01 in Denver, which was themed “Beyond Boundaries,” and focused on moving data across them. “I was a grad student, and I had a demo in the DOE booth demonstrating my master’s thesis, which at that time was to use the Internet to move large amounts of data reliably from one point to the other,” he says. That capability was called reliable file transfer, and, in his words, it “has now transformed into what is called ‘Globus’.” The first tool he helped build moved research data around. The latest one lets the data stay in place. Since SC01, Madduri has been to the conference roughly 20 times and is specific about what he takes home. “I learn parallel processing, how people are scaling AI training, how people are dealing with parallelization, how people are dealing with resource utilization monitoring,” he notes. His group attends the Computational Approaches for Cancer Workshop every year. Lately, the interest has moved to AI agents. “The agentic approaches are the next frontier for us,” he declares. Madduri is also aware that he walks in unusual research domains. Before biomedicine, he worked with high-energy physicists, earthquake engineers, and cosmologists. “When I go to SC, I live in many different worlds,” he says. “I am part of a very small group of people that go to a [combined] human genetics conference and a supercomputing conference.” What Is Still Missing For Madduri, his debt is not settled. More than a decade after the first veterans enrolled, the Million Veteran Program data have produced a map but not yet a cure. What stands between those two things is the work of getting separate institutions to compute as one. To date, that still is being done largely by hand. “For the earlier experiments, it was us talking to NERSC, us talking to Argonne, us talking to Oak Ridge,” Madduri says. “It is a lot of human in the loop.” He is hoping the American Science Cloud being built under the DOE’s Genesis Mission will take that over: “It would be automated, run using APIs.” For now, Madduri remains focused on turning data into triumph, using a very special cohort of data to reveal the next breakthrough against cancer or spare someone a lifetime of anxiety. Until then, he marks progress one good idea, one technical advancement, and one SC Conference at a time. “My connection to Supercomputing, to SC, is long and very fruitful,” Madduri says. “I will be back in November, in Chicago, for SC26.” Join the Conversation at SC26 SC26 brings together the people building the computing infrastructure the work described herein depends on: systems, data platforms, networks, and storage that let research run at scale and across institutions. Attendees engage with technical papers, workshops, tutorials, posters, and Birds of a Feather (BoF) sessions covering AI, quantum computing, and HPC alongside practitioners from national laboratories, industry, and academia working on similar problems. Madduri will also be part of the SC26 Regional Tech Hub, a multimedia forum making its conference debut in Chicago, where he will contribute to the High-throughput Computing Infrastructures and Systems area. Join us in Chicago, November 15–20, 2026, for a week of discovery, collaboration, and community with a spotlight on regional technology leaders. Register today! Supplied by SC26

evening.title: AUKUS: HII Awarded Contract for Engineering and Design Support
evening.text:
HII announced that its Newport News Shipbuilding (NNS) division was awarded a $56 million contract by the U.S. Navy for shipbuilding engineering and design in support of the trilateral Australia, United Kingdom, and United States (AUKUS) partnership.

HII press release

The contract includes an option which, if exercised, would bring the cumulative value of this contract to $91 million. HII continues to take a whole-company approach to support the AUKUS agreement, providing services and support for AUKUS across its business divisions.

Under the contract, in support of Foreign Military Sales (FMS) requirements, NNS will continue supporting the United Kingdom and Australia, including technology insertion, engineering, supply chain and workforce development support, and digital transformation. The award also includes the United States Industry Support (USIS) effort, wherein NNS engineers and designers will support the design of the SSN-AUKUS nuclear-powered submarine to be built by the United Kingdom and Australia.

“Our longstanding nuclear experience at NNS directly benefits the AUKUS mission to support shared security objectives,” said Bryan Caccavale, NNS vice president of program management. “We are honored to leverage that experience and contribute even more to the AUKUS partnership.”

The contract award is the latest in a range of initiatives HII is actively engaged in to advance the AUKUS partnership. HII’s Mission Technologies division in Australia was awarded the contract to deliver the Australian Submarine Supplier Qualification (AUSSQ) Program, which accelerates the identification, development and qualification of Australian suppliers for integration into the United States submarine industrial base.

HII is also working with Australian industry and academia in Australia to develop the skilled workforce needed to support Australia’s nuclear-powered submarine enterprise. This includes educating and training thousands of engineers, maritime specialists, nuclear tradespeople and other professionals to support the enterprise across its full lifecycle.

The company was also awarded the Australian Submarine Agency’s Nuclear Capability Advisory Services (ANCAS) contract in December 2025 to support development of Australia’s Nuclear Power Submarine (NPS) programs through nuclear program management and technical support services.

evening.title: Five Indian Combat Drone Projects Target Different Roles
evening.text:
India’s next generation combat aviation is leaving the realm of pilot-in-control aircraft. Multiple developers are working on concepts for unmanned aircraft which would accompany combat fighters, perform electronic surveillance and strikes in highly contested airspace.
Five programmes stand out from the fray: HAL’s CATS Warrior, NewSpace Research Technologies’ Abhimanyu, DRDO’s Ghataka, Paninian Aerospace’s Svayatt-M1 and AvionX Aerospace’s Vajra. They are not direct competitors, as each has a different target role, varying degrees of development maturity and distinct customer requirements.
HAL Combat Air Teaming System unmanned combat aircraft India
HAL’s Combat Air Teaming System (CATS) unmanned combat aircraft is being developed by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited in partnership with NewSpace Research Technologies and Tata Elxsi. It is intended to operate with manned fighters, supporting them in strike, surveillance and electronic warfare roles. HAL performed an engine ground run of the full scale demonstrator in January 2025, while its latest annual report lists ground runs, taxi tests and flight trials as planned for FY2026-27.
NewSpace Research Technologies Abhimanyu naval collaborative combat aircraft India
Abhimanyu, or the Naval Collaborative Combat Air Vehicle (N-CCAV), is being developed by NewSpace Research Technologies for the Indian Navy under the iDEX Aditi 2.0 framework. Like CATS, it is intended as a force-multiplier for manned naval aviation, performing intelligence-surveillance-reconnaissance, electronic warfare, decoy and strike tasks. NewSpace displayed a half-scale concept model at Aero India 2025. The design-and-development contract for the programme has been signed, but this should not be confused with an actual aircraft.
DRDO SWiFT autonomous flying wing UCAV technology demonstrator India
Ghataka represents a different class of combat aviation. Being developed by DRDO’s aeronautical R&D ecosystem, it is a stealthy flying-wing unmanned combat aircraft which aims to perform deep penetration strike and intelligence gathering. Its autonomous SWiFT technology demonstrator achieved an unassisted flight in July 2022. Apart from that, the full-scale prototype of Ghataka has not been seen, and the reports of a 60-aircraft requirement should not be conflated with actual production.
Paninian Aerospace Svayatt M1 autonomous collaborative combat aircraft concept India
Paninian Aerospace’s Svayatt-M1 is another concept for an autonomous collaborative combat aircraft. The company also develops the Yantur family of turbofan engines with thrust from 3 kN to 12 kN, which can power various kinds of UAVs, including combat aircraft, as well as cruise missiles and aerial targets. As Paninian’s website suggests, these engines are in development, and no production-suitable engines are known to have been fitted to a flying Svayatt-M1.
AvionX Aerospace Vajra naval collaborative combat aerial vehicle concept India
AvionX Aerospace’s Vajra is a naval collaborative combat aerial vehicle concept, which is intended to perform maritime reconnaissance, electronic warfare and precision strikes in conjunction with aircraft carriers. The company lists carrier onboard delivery/deck landing as one of its design drivers, apart from autonomous operations. However, its website’s content is indicative of a developer at best, and no prototype flights or Navy contracts are known to have taken place. (AvionX)
These programs are not comparable in isolation: apart from speed, range and payload, the distance from concept to prototype, flight tests and service entry should be taken into account.
HAL’s CATS Warrior unmanned aircraft has performed a full-scale engine ground run, while Abhimanyu has a government-endorsed development pathway. Ghataka has seen a prototype flight at a reduced scale, and the reports of a 60-aircraft order still await an actual production start. Private defense companies Paninian Aerospace and AvionX develop their own concepts for a naval collaborative combat aircraft. However, none of the programmes have demonstrated their combat utility in prototype flights, let alone production and service entry.
The differences in development approaches stem from varying customer needs: while CATS Warrior is intended to complement the Indian Air Force’s fighter operations, Abhimanyu addresses the requirements of the Indian Navy. Ghataka is a more assertive deep penetration strike aircraft, while private defense developers suggest more generic solutions.

evening.title: Spyware vendors found a way to make targeted ads even worse
evening.text: The online advertising industry has found a new way to make itself even more unpopular, with one adtech outfit accused of helping spyware vendors infect people's phones without them even clicking an ad. Researchers at Citizen Lab say they've uncovered the first publicly confirmed case of a zero-click mercenary spyware attack being delivered through targeted online ads, with devices at Al Jazeera among those infected. The technique, dubbed "AdFection," turns advertising networks into a spyware delivery system. Simply opening a website or app can be enough to trigger the attack, with no suspicious links or downloads involved. Israeli adtech firm Discover-Tech is allegedly behind the operation, according to researchers at Citizen Lab, which says the company acts as a middleman between the online advertising industry and multiple spyware and hacking vendors. "We present technical evidence that the Israel-based company Discover-Tech, while purporting to be a legitimate advertising company, appears to be a front for large-scale ad espionage abuse," the researchers wrote. “In fact, it appears that serving as this bridge is Discover-Tech’s primary purpose." Discover-Tech’s Controlium platform exploits the real-time bidding system that decides which ads appear on websites and apps. Every time someone loads a page, advertisers compete for available ad space and, in the process, receive information about the user's device and location. Discover-Tech allegedly used that data to identify specific targets and serve them malicious ads. One spyware vendor linked to the operation is Candiru, the Israeli developer now known as Integrity Labs. Citizen Lab traced attacks against at least 45 devices at Al Jazeera in 2024 and 2025 to Candiru spyware delivered through ads from Discover-Tech. Discover-Tech didn't have to sneak into the advertising system, as Google and IAB Europe had listed the company as an approved vendor since 2020, apparently unaware of what it was Citizen Lab claims it was doing with that access. Citizen Lab sifted through nearly four billion ad-bidding records and found Discover-Tech ads on more than 70,000 mobile apps and 120,000 websites between March and June 2026. Some reached networks belonging to government agencies, defense organizations, and NATO. Researchers found no evidence that those organizations were infected, but they say the ads could have been used to profile devices on those networks. The researchers said the operation also covertly directed millions of devices toward servers associated with Candiru, although those connections don't necessarily indicate spyware infections. Google has since terminated Discover-Tech's access to its advertising exchanges and removed it from its approved vendor lists. IAB Europe followed suit, while Beeswax, Vungle and Eskimi also took action. Discover-Tech and Candiru did not respond to Citizen Lab's requests for comment, nor ours. The researchers argue that the findings expose serious failings in an advertising industry that allowed a company with links to commercial surveillance operators to operate inside its supposedly vetted ecosystem for years. “Discover-Tech’s mass abuse, privacy invasion, and facilitation for mercenary spyware attacks illustrates structural flaws with the online advertising system, which failed to detect or prevent the abuse documented in this report,” Citizen Lab said. For years, the worst thing about targeted advertising was that it knew far too much about you. Turns out some advertisers were interested in much more than your shopping habits. ®

evening.title: US teen arrested in Illinois for plotting attack on Hindu place of worship
evening.text:
A teenager was arrested for allegedly plotting to carry out a “mass shooting” at a Hindu place of worship in the US state of Illinois, with investigators recovering a manifesto expressing white supremacist ideology and references to violence against people of Indian descent.
Alexandros Paporakis, 19, of Palatine village was arrested on October 11 and charged with making a terrorist threat and unlawful possession of a weapon.
According to investigators, the youth had tried to open fire “potentially targeting” the place of worship in the Aurora city in Illinois, but his gun jammed, forcing him to drive back home, a move that prevented a mass murder.
The specific intended location has not been disclosed by the authorities.
Palatine Police detectives examined electronic communications and a document attributed to Paporakis titled “Why I Fought: A.K.A.: (Aurora Shooter’s Manifesto)”, which contained “statements expressing white supremacist and extremist ideologies, including references to violence directed toward individuals of South Asian heritage, particularly those of Indian descent”.
Detectives believe Paporakis may have been planning to carry out the attack on October 11.
“However, the specific intended location has not been confirmed and remains under investigation,” police said on Wednesday.
The Consulate General of India in Chicago said it appreciated the timely action by law enforcement authorities and was in touch with members of the Indian diaspora while closely monitoring developments.
The arrest comes amid celebrations of Hindu festivals, including Navaratri and Durga Puja, and just two weeks after the Shree Swaminarayan Vadtal Dham Hindu Mandir in Richmond Heights, Ohio, was vandalised.
On October 11, the Palatine Police Department was contacted by the Mount Prospect Police Department regarding information it had received about a potential mass shooting.
The information originated from an individual who reported receiving concerning electronic communications from Paporakis.
According to a report by NBC Chicago, Paporakis had worked as a cashier at fast-food restaurant Taco Bell and had plotted to carry out a “mass shooting of Indian people” at a Hindu temple in Aurora.
He drove to the temple last Sunday “decked out for war”. The day he chose to carry out the carnage at the sprawling place of worship was filled with people. He was “one malfunctioning rifle away from becoming a mass shooter”.
Paporakis showed up “to kill a significant number of Indians”, the report said, quoting police.
Investigators said he had a “modified AR-style rifle and 300 rounds of ammo, enough to fill ten magazines for reloading, along with body armour, gasoline cans” and an assortment of Hakenkreuz (hooked cross used by Nazis), the report said.
Paporakis allegedly drove from his mother’s home in Palatine to the Aurora temple. Authorities said that “he tried to open fire but the gun jammed, so he drove home”.
There he “searched the internet trying to learn how to unjam his gun and called a colleague, informing them of (his) intent to carry out a mass shooting”.
The co-worker then notified the police, informing them of the plot, and Paporakis was arrested Sunday before he could return to the temple.
The youth was arrested as he was leaving his residence following a coordinated response by the Palatine and Mount Prospect police departments.
Paporakis has been charged with one count of making a terrorist threat and one count of unlawful possession of weapons.
He appeared for a detention hearing on Wednesday at the Cook County Third Municipal District Courthouse in Rolling Meadows, where a judge ordered him detained. His next court appearance is scheduled for October 30.
According to investigators, Paporakis “expressed pleasure calling himself a sociopathic white supremacist Neo-Nazi filled with hatred, fantasising about mass murder nearly every day”.
In a social media post, the Hindu American Foundation commended law enforcement for swift action.
“We also urge the community to stay vigilant and report any potential threat. Every community deserves to worship without fear,” it said.
The Coalition of Hindus of North America (CoHNA) said the “disturbing plot” comes as Hindus gather in large numbers to celebrate Navratri, and just two weeks after an attack on a temple in Ohio.
“Hindu temples and all houses of worship must be sanctuaries of peace, prayer, and solace – NEVER targets of hate, violence, or terror. We thank law enforcement for their swift action in averting what could have been an unspeakable tragedy.
“We urge elected officials and law enforcement agencies to take the growing threats against Hindu places of worship seriously, strengthen protections, and unequivocally condemn Hinduphobia,” it said in a social media post.
The group called on temples and community organisations to review their security measures, remain vigilant, and promptly report suspicious activity.
“The freedom to worship without fear is a fundamental American right. It must be protected,” it said.
Police said they were working with the FBI as the investigation continued, including a review of possible additional charges. Authorities have not identified any known ongoing threat to the public associated with the incident.
“The seriousness of this alleged threat cannot be overstated… Protecting our communities and places of worship remains a priority,” Palatine Police Chief William Nord said.
FBI Chicago Special Agent in Charge Ryan Whalen said the agency aggressively works alongside its local and state law enforcement partners to identify, investigate, and dismantle any threats of violence driven by radical ideologies.
